opus-5.5.text:
I think investors are mostly betting on the people and the direction rather than on any particular product.

First, there's the team. Many of us have spent years doing fundamental research: reinforcement learning, planning, reasoning, understanding how these large models actually learn. At this stage of AI, a group that understands the underlying mechanisms deeply is rare. Investors know that whoever makes the next real breakthrough is likely to come from a small group of people who have been thinking about these problems for a long time.

Second, there's the thesis. Scaling has carried the field a long way, but a lot of us believe the next step won't come from simply adding more data and compute. It will come from better algorithms, more efficient training, models that can reason and plan instead of just pattern-matching. If you believe that, a team focused on that question is worth backing early, before a product exists, because by the time a product is obvious, the valuation is much higher.

Third, the market itself has changed. Investors have watched a few AI labs go from zero to enormous value in a very short time. So the logic becomes: a small chance of being one of the few groups that defines the next generation of models is worth a lot, even with high uncertainty. In a sense they're buying an option on the future.

Of course, a valuation isn't an achievement in itself. It's a responsibility. It means people trust that we can turn research insight into something real, and now we have to actually deliver. For me the most important thing is still doing good science. If the understanding is right, the products will follow.

r001.rationale: The response discusses backing a team before a product exists, but does not explain that rapid AI change makes the eventual product hard to specify at the outset.

r002.rationale: It presents the team’s research expertise and focus as reasons for investor confidence, but does not identify the team’s ability to respond quickly to new AI developments.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first, I think it's worth being honest: no one gives you that kind of number because of a slide deck. They give it because of a thesis about where the field is going, and because of the people who are going to execute on it.

The thesis part is this. For the last few years, the industry has been in a scaling era, where progress mostly came from more data, more compute, bigger models. That's been incredibly productive, but everyone can feel it bending. The frontier labs are hitting the limits of what you can scrape from the internet, and the cost of each incremental gain keeps going up. So the question investors are asking is: what's the next lever? My bet, and the bet of the people joining me, is that the next lever is reasoning and search, models that can think for longer, plan, verify their own work, and learn from their own experience rather than only imitating human text. That's a line of research I've been pushing since my time on Go, through OpenGo, and into the work on planning and reasoning in language models at FAIR. If you believe that's the next step change, you don't want to be late to it, and there are very few teams in the world who have actually built those systems end to end.

The people part is maybe more important. In this field, the talent is extremely concentrated. There are a handful of people who have trained frontier-scale systems, who understand both the theory and the engineering, and who can attract others like them. When a team like that forms, capital shows up, partly because the investors know the alternative is that this team goes somewhere else. And the capital requirements are real. You cannot do serious research at the frontier with a few GPUs anymore. If you're going to take a shot at this, you need enough compute to run real experiments from day one, otherwise you spend two years catching up and the window closes.

So I'd reframe it a bit. The valuation isn't a statement that we already have a product worth that much. It's a statement about the size of the opportunity and the cost of competing for it. It also comes with a lot of pressure. I don't think any of us treat the number as something we've earned yet. It's closer to an expectation we now have to live up to, and the only way to do that is to actually show that this approach produces something people can use.

r001.rationale: The response discusses changing research trends and the next lever in AI, but does not say rapid change makes it difficult to specify the startup’s eventual product at the outset.

r002.rationale: The response cites the team’s expertise and ability to execute as reasons for investor confidence, but does not identify quick responsiveness to new AI developments as a central basis.

astra-6.text:
I can’t speak for each investor, but I think they were betting on the team and the opportunity. Before there’s a product, the question is whether this group has the technical judgment to identify a promising direction and the ability to execute on it. In AI, that can matter a lot because the technology is moving so quickly.

But I’d separate valuation from validation. A valuation reflects expectations about what you might build; it doesn’t establish that the technology works or that customers will want it. You still have to turn that confidence into something useful.

r001.rationale: The response says AI technology is moving quickly, but does not explain that this makes the eventual product difficult to specify at the outset.

r002.rationale: It cites the team’s technical judgment and ability to execute, but does not identify responding quickly to new AI developments as a central basis for investor confidence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think investors are betting on the team and the direction, rather than on an existing product. In AI, a lot of the hard work happens before you have something customers can use: assembling the research team, securing compute, and testing whether your ideas actually work. So the investment gives you the resources to do that work.

But I wouldn’t confuse a valuation with validation. It reflects expectations about what the company could become. You still have to turn those expectations into technical progress and, eventually, something people find valuable.
